content.title: The Great Energy Dilemma: Paradoxes of Sustainable Development
content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation

content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

Energy represent both an immense opportunity for development and a challenge for preserving life on Earth.

It powers the lights in our homes, the machines in our hospitals, and the growth of entire economies. Yet the way we produce and consume energy, overwhelmingly through fossil fuels, has created major environmental and climate issue that endanger opportunities for development.

This is the great energy dilemma of our time: we must expand energy access to lift billions out of poverty while simultaneously slashing emissions to preserve a livable planet.

Can we do both urgently, equitably, and at scale?

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

concepts.title: energy for development
concepts.body: Energy for development refers to the provision and use of energy resources to support economic growth, improve living standards, and enhance social well-being in communities, particularly in developing regions.

concepts.title: energy trilemma
concepts.body: The energy trilemma refers to the challenge of balancing three key objectives in energy policy: ensuring energy security, promoting environmental sustainability, and providing energy equity or affordability for all consumers.

concepts.title: paris agreement goals
concepts.body: The Paris Agreement goals refer to the international commitments made by countries to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius, and to enhance the ability to adapt to climate change impacts.

content.text:
This lesson unpacks the twin imperatives of development and climate action, and the deep contradictions they expose in today’s energy system.

Why does the Global South, rich in renewable potential, receive only a sliver of clean energy investment?

How can we justify a world where the same fossil-fueled growth model that built wealth for some now threatens the survival of others?


We invite you to explore these paradoxes that will shape the future of humanity. This lesson challenges you to think beyond false choices, between growth and sustainability, between rich and poor, between climate goals and development rights, and toward an energy transition that is just, inclusive, and transformative.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: A: Development and Climate: The Twin Challenges

content.text:
We live in a world shaped—and strained—by energy.
On the one hand, energy is the lifeblood of development: powering homes, schools, hospitals, economies. On the other, the way we produce and use energy is damaging our planet and ecosystems, threatening the very foundations of life itself.

This is the defining paradox of our time. We need more energy to ensure every person can live a dignified, healthy life. But we also need cleaner energy immediately to avert catastrophic climate change. These two goals are both non-negotiable. Yet they are pulling against each other in a world still structured by deep inequalities, outdated infrastructure, and powerful fossil fuel interests.


The paradox of sustainable development lies on these two main elements that are indissociable from each other and critical to understand the most significant challenges of our times.

content.quote:
“We face a moment of truth,
Close to 760 million people still lack access to electricity.
Some 2.6 billion people lack access to clean cooking solutions.
And how we produce and use energy is the main cause of the climate crisis.”
content.author: UN Secretary-General António Guterres, November 2021

content.text: Note: The exact numbers for people lacking access to energy and <ai prompt="Clarify clean cooking.">clean cooking 💬️</ai> have changed since the date of this Declaration.
1 : Energy powers development
There is no development without energy

To better understand this relationship, we often look at the human development index 💬️ (HDI), a measure that gives us a snapshot of a nation's overall well-being. The HDI is a composite indicator consisting of life expectancy, education and per capita income indicators. Countries are scored between 0 and 1, with higher scores reflecting greater development.

Energy consumption is closely tied to HDI.

At low levels of development, even small increases in energy use lead to significant improvements in HDI. However, as development increases, additional energy use has diminishing returns, with smaller improvements in HDI at higher levels of energy consumption. While it’s important to note that the relationship is not as strong at very high levels of HDI – after a certain threshold, more energy use doesn’t guarantee higher levels of development – it is still crucial to understand that historically, no country has achieved a high level of development without increased energy use.

content.text: 2: Today’s energy systems exacerbate Climate Change

content.quote: Energy is the dominant contributor to climate change which affects human development.

content.text:
The very fuel that powered industrial development is now accelerating a global crisis. Fossil fuels—coal, oil, and gas—still make up more the majority of the world’s energy supply, despite decades of climate warnings. As a result, energy production and use now account for about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions due to the combustion of fossil fuels for electricity, heat, and transport.

This presents a significant challenge for sustainable development, as the impacts of climate change, such as extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and shifting agricultural patterns, undermine economic stability, food security, and public health.

These effects disproportionately affect the poorest and most vulnerable populations, who are least equipped to adapt and have contributed the least to global emissions. As a result, climate change exacerbates existing inequalities and poses a direct threat to development gains, particularly in low-income and climate-vulnerable countries.

metadata.title: Energy and Climate Change
metadata.footnote: Pie chart showing the sources of GHG emissions by sector in 2021. Energy includes Electricity and Heat, Manufacturing and Construction, Transportation, Fugitive Emissions, and Buildings

content.text:
The dual challenge of expanding energy access and addressing climate change, the twin imperatives of sustainable energy, is at the heart of the development agenda.

 Energy is essential for economic growth, education, healthcare, and broader human development. Yet, the way the world has historically powered development—through fossil fuels—is now destabilizing the climate and putting those very development gains at risk.

Emerging economies are rightly seeking to grow, industrialize, and prosper. But if this growth follows the same fossil-fueled path of the past, climate goals will collapse and the poorest will once again suffer the most.

So we face a tricky equation: the same systems that deny energy to the poor are also destabilizing the climate.

This also raises urgent questions:

content.title: Who gets to industrialize, and how?
Can the right to develop be realized without deepening the climate crisis?
And can we build a new energy system that both powers prosperity and protects the planet?

content.text:
The answers lie in reimagining development not as a trade-off between growth and sustainability, but as a transformational opportunity to leapfrog into cleaner, more resilient energy systems that are aligned with climate goals and grounded in justice.

Here, the term leapfrog refers to the process by which emerging markets fulfil their growing energy demand and get closer to their development goals from non fossil sources, thus bypassing the intermediary stage of building a fossil fuel based energy infrastructure.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: B: Progress and Paradoxes in the Push for Just Energy Transitions

content.text:
The global energy transition is gaining momentum, but beneath the surface of progress lies a series contradiction.

Solar and wind are breaking records. Clean technologies are cheaper and spreading faster than ever before.

And yet, fossil fuels remain deeply entrenched, access remains deeply unequal, and investment flows continue to bypass the communities that need them most.

Are we truly transitioning or just rearranging the imbalance? Why is clean energy booming while fossil fuels still dominate? These questions are crucial to frame the issue of energy for development 💬️ and question the systems at play in its transformation.
Progress: Clean energy is accelerating

Faced with the dual challenge of balancing universal, affordable access with climate mitigation, the world is slowly starting to shift energy systems.

The cost of solar electricity has dropped by over 85% between 2010 and 2020 (IRENA, 2022), and renewables are now the cheapest source of new power in most of the world. In 2024, clean energy investments reached a historic $2 trillion, more than doubling since 2020 (IEA, 2024). As illustrated in the following chart, the share of renewable energy in global electricity generation has already risen from approximately 20% in 2000 to over 30% in 2023. Looking ahead, it is projected to increase by an additional 90% by 2030, compared to 2023 levels.

Solar and wind are finally outcompeting coal and gas in many markets. For the first time, renewables are set to become the largest source of global electricity.

Governments, companies, and communities around the world are increasingly committing to net-zero pathways. Breakthroughs in battery storage 💬️, green hydrogen, and energy access solutions offer hope. These are signs of genuine transformation.

But is it happening fast enough?
Paradox: Fossil Fuels are still dominant
Despite some progress, the underlying energy system is still structurally unjust, carbon-heavy, and deeply unequal.

For decades, fossil fuels like coal, oil, and gas have been the primary sources of energy for electricity, transportation, and industrial processes.

Since 1950, fossil fuel consumption has surged—growing eightfold—and has nearly doubled since 1980. While coal use has declined in many regions, oil and gas consumption continues to rise rapidly.

However, these energy practices raise several concerns:

content.body: Energy consumption disparities and unequal access to resources and economic growth across nations
Negative environmental and health impacts from emissions
Global instability affecting energy supply security and price fluctuations.

content.text: The Contradictions That Still Define the Energy System

The rapid rise of renewables alongside the persistence of fossil fuels highlights key contradictions at the heart of the challenges shaping the quest for just energy transitions in the context of development. Let’s look at some of the most striking paradoxes that define today’s energy transition.

content.title:
Clean energy is cheaper than ever—solar costs dropped >85% since 2010,
Yet fossil fuels still make up 80% of global energy (Energy Institute, 2024).

The Global South holds 70% of renewable potential (RMI, 2024) ,
But emerging markets and developing economies outside of China attracts only 15% of clean energy investment (IEA, 2024).

Global energy intensity—an indicator of efficiency—improved by 2% in 2022, the fastest rate since 2015 (IEA, 2023).
Yet global energy demand rose by 2.2% in 2024 (IEA, 2025).

Global investments in the energy transition reached a record $2 trillion in 2024.
Yet fossil fuel subsidies exceeded $620 billion in 2023 (IEA, 2024).

Africa, is home to 20% of the world’s population, and 80% of all people lacking electricity access (UNSDG, 2025),
Yet the continent receives just under 2% of global clean energy investment, despite vast solar and wind resources (IEA, 2025).

content.text: These contradictions are not just technical, they reflect political, financial, and ethical challenges.
Here again, these paradoxes prompt some questions, and invite us to pause and reflect on the way our world uses energy

content.title: How do we move from incremental change to transformative justice in the energy system?
What kind of development is possible without energy—and what kind of energy supports equitable development?
What would a truly just energy transition look like?

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: C: Powering the Future: Will We Get It Right?

content.text: Part 3 Overview

The challenge with achieving a just energy transition 💬️ is that it has dual imperatives and multiple contradictions. How do we move beyond the current structure and build a system that is beneficial for people, planet and prosperity?

This section explores the foundational shifts required to transition from today’s outdated, fossil-fueled energy systems to a future that is clean, inclusive, and climate-aligned. It begins by diagnosing the limitations of our current centralized energy model, one that disproportionately benefits the wealthy, remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, and suffers from significant inefficiencies and sectoral vulnerabilities.

It then presents the energy system we need: one that is renewable, non-polluting, and designed to deliver cross-sectoral development gains, from health and education to food security and resilience.

Finally, it outlines key levers for transformative change in the coming decade. This section sets the stage for understanding that the energy transition is not just a technological upgrade, it is a political, social, and moral imperative.
Where We Are: A System Built for the Past

Our current energy system is laregely failing the future. It is centralized, fossil-fueled, and disproportionately serves those who already have the most.
As illustrated in the following, charts, several observations can be made about our current energy systems

content.title: Fossil fuels dominate
content.body: Oil, coal, and natural gas are the largest primary energy sources.

content.title: Energy losses
content.body: Gray areas show energy lost during transformation and transmission. Energy losses are a form of inefficiency as they represent energy that is produced but not used for its intended purpose.

content.title: Sector dependencies
content.body:
- Transport relies heavily on oil
- Industry uses a mix of sources, including coal and natural gas
- Buildings depend on electricity and direct fuel use

content.text: Note: An energy system is a set of processes that transforms primary resources, such as fossil fuels or renewable energy resources like solar, wind or hydro, into usable energy forms like electricity to meet human needs. These processes involve several key stages: energy generation, storage, transportation, conversion, and utilization. The global energy flows diagram highlights the sources, how energy is transformed, and where it is used across different sectors.
Where We Need to Go: Building a Just and Climate-Aligned Energy System

To reach universal energy access and climate goals, we need to completely reimagine how energy is produced, distributed, and used.

The energy system we need is:

content.title: Renewable
content.body: Powered by solar, wind, hydro, and green fuels—aligned with a 1.5°C future.

content.title: Clean
content.body: A system that does not create harmful pollution and greenhouse gases.

content.title: Inclusive
content.body: Designed to serve the energy-poor, empower women, and create livelihoods.

content.title: Cross-sectoral
content.body: Delivering integrated development gains, from health and food security to education and climate resilience.

content.text: How Do We Get There
The next decade is decisive. Infrastructure decisions made today will shape the lives of generations to come. So what must we do?

content.title: Position decentralized renewables as core development infrastructure, not just a climate solution.
Scale up digital, data, and AI to improve access, efficiency, and equity in energy systems.
Close the finance gap by building pipelines of bankable projects that deliver multiple benefits from powering rural clinics and schools to preserving biodiversity and boosting food systems.
Align public policy, regulation, and private capital toward inclusive, climate-compatible energy futures.

content.text:
As we have learned in this lesson, a just energy transition is not just a technical challenge. It’s a question of power, values, and urgency. The energy transition will not succeed unless it works for everyone, especially those historically left behind.

In the rest of the module, we’ll dive deeper into how we got here, what needs to change, and we can lead the charge toward a just, inclusive, and sustainable energy future.
Achieving universal energy access and net zero emissions by 2050 will require nothing short of the complete transformation of the global energy system.

content.title: Key Takeaways

takeaways.title: Energy is essential for development, but the way we produce and use it threatens that very goal. Reliable, affordable energy powers everything from healthcare and education to jobs and economic growth. Yet the global energy system—still overwhelmingly fossil-fueled—is the primary driver of climate change. This twin imperative is the defining challenge of our time, especially for low-income and climate-vulnerable countries.

Despite progress, our current system is includes paradoxes that hold us back. Clean energy investment is growing fast. But fossil fuels still dominate global energy supply, and the communities most in need receive the smallest share of investment. These contradictions reflect not just technical gaps but deep political and financial imbalances.

A just energy future is possible but it demands bold, systemic change. To build an energy system that delivers for both people and planet, we need to shift toward renewable, inclusive infrastructure supported by digital innovation and fair financing.
